title: Universal Scaling of the Little-Parks Oscillation Amplitude
authors: Yuelin Shen, Zixuan Huang, Xiaoying Xu, Wei Qin, Yufan Li
abstract: The Little-Parks effect played a pivotal role in establishing fluxoid quantization in doubly connected superconductors and providing early evidence for electron pairing, central to BCS theory. More recently, it has emerged as an important phase-sensitive probe of superconducting order. Yet the amplitude of the Little-Parks oscillation has never been fully understood theoretically, as the conventional mean-field Ginzburg-Landau description does not account for its pronounced temperature dependence. Here, we develop a universal theoretical framework incorporating thermal fluctuations in reduced-dimensional superconducting rings. By analyzing Little-Parks measurements across multiple superconductors, we show that the resulting scaling quantitatively captures the temperature-dependent oscillation amplitudes over a broad range of materials and device geometries, resolving the long-standing discrepancy between theory and experiment.
summary: This paper resolves the theoretical puzzle surrounding the temperature dependence of the Little-Parks oscillation amplitude in superconducting rings. By developing a universal framework that accounts for thermal fluctuations via thermally activated phase slips, the authors successfully reconcile theoretical predictions with experimental measurements across various superconducting materials. This provides a robust scaling law for understanding superconducting phase-sensitive probes.
main_problem: The theoretical understanding of the temperature-dependent amplitude of the Little-Parks oscillation remains incomplete, as conventional mean-field theories fail to capture its observed strong temperature variation.
main_result: The authors developed a universal theoretical framework incorporating thermally activated phase slips that successfully scales the oscillation amplitude across diverse superconducting materials, resolving a long-standing theoretical-experimental discrepancy.
method: The analysis involves deriving the oscillation amplitude by modeling the resistance using an activated form that includes both thermodynamic and kinetic energy contributions, leading to a universal scaling law.
model_or_system: The study focuses on doubly connected superconducting rings exhibiting Little-Parks oscillations. The theory builds upon the Ginzburg-Landau framework by incorporating thermally activated phase slips (TAPS) into the resistance calculation.
key_observables: Little-Parks oscillation amplitude ($\Delta T_C$) and the magnetoresistance oscillations $R(T, \Phi)$.
important_parameters: Coherence length ($\xi_0$), ring radius ($r$), critical temperature ($T_C$), and the temperature-dependent scaling function $\chi(t)$.
main_assumptions: The dominant contribution to the resistance in the Little-Parks experiments is assumed to come from thermally activated phase slips, and the conventional GL description is insufficient.
figures_summary: Figures show measured Little-Parks oscillations in various superconductors (Nb, cuprates) demonstrating strong temperature variation, which are then fitted using the derived universal scaling law to extract material parameters.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the failure of conventional GL theory, then develops a new theoretical framework incorporating TAPS, derives the universal scaling law, and finally applies this law to fit and compare data from multiple superconducting materials.
why_interesting: The incorporation of thermal fluctuations (TAPS) into the superconducting order parameter dynamics provides a mechanism to explain temperature dependence in superconducting response, which is relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in quantum materials.
